result: Past rewards bias future perceptual choices specifically when the previous decision was difficult and confidence was low. This confidence-dependent choice updating persists after correcting for slow fluctuations in side bias, indicating active trial-by-trial learning rather than passive drift.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10 provide direct empirical evidence from rat olfactory experiments showing that choice updating is strongest after difficult previous trials (p=0.0002), minimal after easy previous trials, and minimal for easy current trials regardless of previous difficulty. Claim C14 confirms this effect survives normalization for slow bias drift (p=0.003). The statistical evidence and experimental controls strongly support this core finding.

result: Confidence-dependent choice updating is observed across six datasets from four laboratories, spanning rats, mice, and humans, and across olfactory, auditory, and visual modalities. All subjects showed asymptotic performance with low bias and lapse rates, yet exhibited significant choice updating dependent on previous trial difficulty.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 establish asymptotic performance in rats (14/16 rats, p>0.1 for stability). Claims C24-C30 document similar patterns across rat auditory (p=0.007), mouse auditory (p=0.01), mouse visual (p=0.001), and human visual (p<0.05) tasks. The consistency of statistical significance across diverse experimental paradigms, species, and sensory modalities provides strong convergent evidence for the generality of the phenomenon.

result: A normalization procedure successfully distinguishes active trial-by-trial choice updating from slow, non-specific drift in decision boundaries. Slow drift produces apparent updating that is cancelled by subtracting psychometric shifts from trial t-1, while active learning produces shifts specific to trial t that persist after normalization.
evaluation: Claim C12 demonstrates through simulation that slow drift produces non-specific correlations across trials. Claim C13 provides the conceptual framework for why subtraction isolates active learning. Claim C14 provides empirical validation that the effect remains significant (p=0.003) after normalization. The combination of simulation validation, conceptual justification, and empirical confirmation supports this methodological result.

result: A reinforcement learning model incorporating belief states (representing perceptual confidence) successfully accounts for confidence-dependent choice updating, while classical MDP TDRL models without belief states fail to reproduce this pattern. The key difference is that belief-based models scale prediction errors by confidence, producing larger updates after difficult decisions.
evaluation: Claims C15-C16 show the belief-based TDRL model reproduces observed updating patterns through confidence-scaled prediction errors. Claims C17 and C21 demonstrate that MDP TDRL models without belief states show difficulty-independent updating. The model simulations (Figure 3) provide clear qualitative and quantitative matches to behavioral data, supporting the mechanistic explanation.

result: Alternative explanations for choice updating—including MDP TDRL with slow drift or win-stay strategies—fail to account for confidence-dependent updating after normalization. These models produce updating patterns that are either removed by normalization or independent of previous trial difficulty.
evaluation: Claim C18 shows that MDP TDRL with drift loses apparent updating after normalization (Figure 3d). Claim C19 demonstrates that win-stay strategies produce difficulty-independent effects (Figure 3e). These control simulations effectively rule out alternative explanations and strengthen the case for confidence-dependent mechanisms.

result: An on-line Bayesian Support Vector Machine classifier that updates decision boundaries in proportion to classification confidence (margin) produces choice updating patterns similar to the belief-based RL model, providing an alternative computational account.
evaluation: Claim C22 presents SVM simulations (Figure 4b,c) showing similar updating patterns to the TDRL model. Claim C23 generalizes this to statistical classifiers that weight updates by confidence. While the SVM model provides an alternative framework, the simulations demonstrate qualitative similarity to both the TDRL model and behavioral data, supporting this as a viable alternative mechanism.

result: Choice updating transfers across sensory modalities in rats performing randomly interleaved auditory and olfactory decisions. Rats updated olfactory choices after difficult auditory trials (p=0.008) and vice versa (p=0.01), indicating updating occurs in action-value space rather than stimulus-specific coordinates.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33 provide direct statistical evidence for cross-modality transfer with significant p-values. Claim C34 shows updating is present across all transition types but strongest within-modality. Claims C35-C36 provide the inference that this pattern supports action-value updating over stimulus-coordinate updating. The cross-modality transfer is a strong test that distinguishes RL from classifier models, and the data support the RL interpretation.

result: Individual variability in choice updating correlates with task performance: updating is strongest in well-trained subjects with low lapse rates (p=0.03 negative correlation), but shows no relationship with psychometric slope (p=0.21). Some individuals show negligible or opposite updating patterns.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 document the distribution of updating indices across individuals (Figure 10a). Claims C39-C41 provide statistical analyses showing significant correlation with lapse rate but not slope. Claim C42 synthesizes these findings. The statistical evidence is clear, though the correlation with lapse rate is weak (p=0.03), and the interpretation that updating is strongest in well-trained subjects is reasonable but somewhat circular given that low lapse rates define good training.

result: Post-error behavioral effects are highly variable across subjects and datasets, unlike the consistent post-correct updating. RL model simulations show that post-error patterns depend on the dominant noise source: high sensory noise produces minimal updating, while high internal noise (learning rate) produces systematic post-error updating.
evaluation: Claim C43 documents the empirical variability in post-error effects (Figure 11). Claims C44-C45 show model simulations with different noise parameters produce different post-error patterns. Claim C46 notes that post-correct predictions are robust across noise conditions. The model provides a principled explanation for the observed variability, though the low number of error trials limits strong conclusions about individual patterns.

result: Reinforcement learning mechanisms remain engaged even after extensive training (3-4 months), producing systematic choice adjustments in well-learned perceptual decisions. This ongoing learning persists despite asymptotic performance levels.
evaluation: Claim C6 establishes asymptotic performance (14/16 rats, p>0.1 for stability over sessions). Claim C61 notes updating persists after 3-4 months of training. Claim C4 synthesizes this into the conclusion about continual RL engagement. The persistence of updating despite stable psychometric parameters supports this interpretation, though the authors acknowledge this learning might eventually disappear with even more extended training.

result: Confidence-guided choice updating, while suboptimal in laboratory settings with independent trials, can be optimal in natural environments where decision boundaries may shift over time or events are temporally correlated. This reveals joint contributions of perceptual and reinforcement learning processes.
evaluation: Claims C47-C49 present theoretical arguments about optimality in natural vs. laboratory settings. While the reasoning is plausible and supported by citation to Yu and Cohen (2008), these are speculative interpretations rather than empirically tested hypotheses. The manuscript provides no direct evidence that the observed updating is actually optimal in natural settings or that decision boundaries are unstable in the animals' experience. This remains an interesting but unvalidated theoretical framework.

result: Previous rewards bias choices toward the previously rewarded side (F=29.8, p=0.001), but this effect does not alter psychometric sensitivity or lapse rates (p>0.1), indicating the updating specifically affects decision bias rather than perceptual processing or attention.
evaluation: Claim C7 provides strong statistical evidence for the basic choice repetition effect. Claim C11 rules out effects on other psychometric parameters. This establishes that the updating is specific to bias rather than reflecting changes in sensory processing or attention, which is important for interpreting the mechanism.

result: Choice updating is stronger after two consecutive rewarded difficult trials in the same direction compared to one rewarded difficult trial, as predicted by the RL model and confirmed in rat behavior.
evaluation: Claim C62 presents both model prediction and empirical confirmation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b). This provides additional validation of the model's quantitative predictions beyond the main updating effect. However, the manuscript does not provide statistical tests for this comparison, limiting the strength of the conclusion.

result: Animals may employ a mixture of two learning strategies: one updating values in action space and one tracking stimulus identity and statistics across trials. This interpretation is suggested by the observation that within-modality updating is stronger than cross-modality updating.
evaluation: Claim C64 is explicitly speculative ("might point to the fact") and is based on the difference between within- and cross-modality updating strength (C34). While this is a reasonable interpretation of the pattern, no direct evidence is provided for a mixture model, and alternative explanations (e.g., partial generalization across modalities) are not ruled out. This remains an interesting hypothesis for future work.

result: Prior literature documents that outcomes bias perceptual decisions, and reinforcement learning theory predicts that difficult, low-confidence decisions provide greater learning opportunities than easy decisions because outcomes are less predictable.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 accurately cite extensive prior literature on trial history effects. Claims C52-C53 present standard predictions from RL theory under uncertainty, supported by citations to Lak et al. 2017, 2019. These claims appropriately contextualize the current work within existing literature and theory.

result: Prior neurophysiological studies show that dopamine neurons encode confidence-dependent prediction errors during perceptual decisions, predict subsequent choice biases, and causally influence psychometric curves when manipulated. Frontal cortical regions (mPFC, OFC) also likely contribute to confidence-guided updating.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 accurately cite prior work (Lak et al. 2017, 2019; Hirokawa et al. 2019) establishing neural substrates. These citations are appropriate and accurately represent the cited work. However, these are not new findings from the current manuscript but rather contextualization of the behavioral results within existing neural evidence.

result: Confidence-dependent learning differs from other sequential effects including priming of popout, is consistent with predictions from Bayesian drift-diffusion models, and requires trial feedback unlike some other sequential choice effects.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 appropriately distinguish the current findings from related phenomena through citations to relevant literature (Maljkovic & Nakayama 1994; Drugowitsch et al. 2019; Braun et al. 2018; Glaze et al. 2015). These distinctions are important for positioning the work but represent literature review rather than new empirical findings.
